name: EQ01 the window's timer is never started
why: an unbroken stream is never evaluated until it ends; the window record exists but holds no timer

name: EQ02 the trailing timer's callback leaves the window open
why: the window's timer outlives the run the trailing timer made and fires a second run a maximum wait after the first event, with no state waiting

name: EQ03 every schedule restarts the window
why: the window never reaches its end while events keep coming less than a delay apart: the maximum wait does not bound anything

name: EQ04 the window is armed twice
why: a second window timer nobody tracks fires a maximum wait after the first event and runs the key again, after the state was evaluated by the tracked one

name: EQ05 the window is never recorded
why: every schedule arms a new window timer and none is ever cleared: more than two timers wait, and each runs the key

name: EQ06 a run leaves the window in the table
why: after the first run through the window's timer the table still holds the entry, so no later schedule opens a window and a second unbroken stream is never evaluated until it ends

name: EQ07 the window's callback leaves the trailing timer running
why: the trailing timer, whose handle the run forgets, fires after the window's run and runs the key again with no state waiting (a pending timer and nothing unevaluated)

name: EQ08 a run leaves the trailing handle in the table
why: the next schedule of the key clears a handle that is no longer a pending timer; seen only by the fake clock's stale-clear counter

name: EQ09 closing a window does not clear its timer
why: the window's timer outlives the run the trailing timer made, or the cancel, and fires a second run with no state waiting

name: EQ10 cancel leaves the window open
why: an immediate evaluation (an editor switch) or a closed document in the middle of a stream leaves the window's timer, which fires a run with no state waiting

name: EQ11 the window's timer is asked for the delay
why: a stream is evaluated every delay and not every maximum wait: a run comes neither a delay after the last event nor a maximum wait after the first

name: EQ12 the window's timer is asked for the maximum wait plus the delay
why: the unevaluated state is older than the maximum wait when the window runs it

name: EQ13 the window's timer is asked for one millisecond less than the maximum wait
why: the window runs a millisecond before the maximum wait after the first event: no unevaluated state is ever older than the maximum wait, so only the timing rule (a run comes a delay after the last event or a maximum wait after the first) sees it

name: EQ14 the cell-context scheduler does not hand the maximum wait on
why: the cell-context key is a pure trailing debounce: an unbroken stream of keystrokes leaves it stale until the stream ends

name: EQ15 the cell-context scheduler cancels the pending evaluation before each debounced event
why: every document event and every selection event after an edit closes the window: the window restarts at each event, as in EQ03, but through the scheduler

name: EQ16 evaluateNow leaves the pending evaluation
why: an editor switch evaluates at once and leaves the trailing timer and the window: both fire later and evaluate again with nothing waiting

name: EQ17 a window opens only while no other key waits
why: with two documents edited together the second one's window is missing: its stream is evaluated by the first one's window or not at all, and its own run does not come a maximum wait after its first edit

name: EQ18 the cell-background decorator's wiring copy leaves the maximum wait out
from: const typing = createKeyedDebouncer({ timers: clock, delayMs: TYPING_DEBOUNCE_MS, maxWaitMs: TYPING_MAX_WAIT_MS });
to: const typing = createKeyedDebouncer({ timers: clock, delayMs: TYPING_DEBOUNCE_MS });
why: the copy of how `registerCellBackgroundFeature` builds its debouncer is the pure trailing one: the tint of a document edited in an unbroken stream is not re-applied until the stream ends

name: EQ19 the cell-context wiring copy leaves the maximum wait out
why: the copy of how `registerExecutionFeature` builds its scheduler is the pure trailing one: the key is not re-evaluated until the stream ends

name: EQ20 the cell-background decorator's wiring copy does not cancel a closed document's pending run
from: typing.cancel(docA.uri.toString()); // onDidCloseTextDocument (the old code had no such handler)
why: the closed document's trailing timer and window stay and fire a refresh nobody is waiting for (a timer pending with no state to evaluate)

name: EQ21 the window's callback closes the window instead of dropping the trailing timer
why: the window clears its own, already fired, timer and leaves the trailing one, which fires a second run with no state waiting; the clear of a timer that is not pending is seen by the fake clock's counter too

name: EQ22 closing a window leaves its record in the table
why: after a cancel (an editor switch, a closed document) the table still holds the cleared window, so the next stream opens none and is evaluated only when it ends

name: EQ23 cancel closes the windows of every key
why: closing one document in the middle of another's stream drops the other's window: its stream is evaluated only when it ends

name: EQ24 dropping a trailing timer leaves its handle in the table
why: after a cancel the next drop clears a handle that is not a pending timer; seen only by the fake clock's stale-clear counter

name: EQ25 the window's timer is asked for twice the maximum wait
why: the unevaluated state of an unbroken stream is twice the maximum wait old when the window runs it

name: EQ26 a window runs the first run it was opened with
why: argued equivalent HERE: both worlds hand the debouncer a run that reads the live state when it runs (the scheduler's `evaluate`, the tint's refresh of every visible editor), so the first run and the latest are the same function of the world; `s343-max-wait.test.ts` kills it with runs that differ
